The anchor count, about 200,000 for a typical 800 × 1333 COCO input, shows why the class imbalance is so severe. The last lines show the inference API of TorchVision's detection models: the model takes a list of images of any size and returns, per image, a dictionary of boxes, labels and scores after its own NMS. With weights="DEFAULT" it loads COCO-trained weights; those were not available offline, so the randomly initialised model here returns 100 meaningless boxes; the point of running it is to confirm the input and output format.

2.4 Anchor-based and anchor-free methods

An anchor-based detector places a fixed set of reference boxes at every position, for example three scales × three aspect ratios in RetinaNet and Faster R-CNN, and learns to classify each anchor and regress offsets from it to a ground-truth box [53,58]. Training needs an assignment rule: the Faster R-CNN RPN labels an anchor positive if its IoU with some ground-truth box is at least 0.7 (or it is the best anchor for that box) and negative below 0.3 [53]; RetinaNet uses 0.5 and 0.4 [58]. Box targets are encoded relative to the anchor, using the centre offset divided by the anchor size and the log of the size ratio (the encode/decode pair above). Anchors bring hyperparameters (sizes, ratios, IoU thresholds) that must suit the dataset.

Anchor-free detectors predict boxes from points. CornerNet detects the top-left and bottom-right corners as keypoint heatmaps and groups them with learned embeddings [59]. CenterNet ("objects as points") predicts a heatmap of object centres per class, plus the box width and height (and a sub-pixel offset) at each centre; peaks are extracted with a 3 × 3 max-pool, which replaces box NMS [60]. FCOS treats every location inside a box as a positive and regresses the four distances (l, t, r, b) to the box sides, with a "centre-ness" branch that down-weights low-quality predictions far from the centre [61]. ATSS then showed that, once the definition of positive and negative training samples is aligned, anchor-based and anchor-free detectors perform almost identically: the essential difference is how training samples are selected, not whether anchors exist [62].

Detection as set prediction. DETR removed both anchors and NMS. A transformer decoder turns a fixed number of learned queries (100) into predictions, and training uses a bipartite (Hungarian) matching between predictions and ground truth [63,64], so each object is supervised by exactly one prediction and duplicates are penalised by the loss itself. DETR matched a tuned Faster R-CNN on COCO but needed long training schedules and was weak on small objects; Deformable DETR attends to a small set of sampled points around a reference, which improved small-object accuracy and needed about ten times fewer training epochs [65].

2.5 Post-processing: non-maximum suppression

Dense detectors fire many overlapping boxes on each object. Greedy NMS keeps the highest-scoring box, deletes every remaining box whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold (commonly 0.5–0.7), and repeats. Its weakness is crowds: two genuinely overlapping people can suppress each other. Soft-NMS decays the scores of overlapping boxes instead of deleting them, which improved COCO AP for both two-stage and one-stage detectors without retraining [66]. Try the trade-off below.

Solid boxes survive NMS, faint boxes are suppressed. The two overlapping people on the right (ground truth dashed) have IoU 0.52: a threshold below that deletes one of them, a high threshold lets duplicates on the left survive.

Box regression losses also moved toward IoU. Smooth-L1 on encoded offsets treats the four coordinates independently, while IoU-based losses optimise the evaluation quantity directly; generalised IoU adds a penalty based on the smallest enclosing box so that the loss still has a gradient when the boxes do not overlap [67].

2.6 Real-time detection

Real-time usually means at least 30 frames per second end to end on the target hardware, including resizing, inference and post-processing. The YOLO line became the reference family: YOLOv4 combined a set of training techniques ("bag of freebies") and architectural modules [68]; YOLOX moved to an anchor-free design with a decoupled classification/regression head and dynamic label assignment [69]; YOLOv7 refined re-parameterised architectures and assignment [70]; YOLOv10 trained with a one-to-one assignment branch alongside the usual one-to-many branch so that inference can drop NMS [71]. RT-DETR showed that a DETR-style detector with an efficient hybrid encoder can beat comparably sized YOLO models in both speed and accuracy, in part because it avoids NMS, whose run time varies with the number of boxes [72]. On the backbone side, depthwise-separable convolutions (MobileNets) [73] and compound scaling with weighted bidirectional feature pyramids (EfficientDet) [74] trade accuracy against compute along a smooth curve.

The practical levers, roughly in order of effect, are input resolution (cost grows with pixel count, while small objects need pixels), backbone width and depth, numeric precision (FP16 or INT8), and post-processing cost. The production-engineering article in this series covers export, quantisation and latency measurement in depth.

2.7 Results on the toy world

The multi-task network of §7 includes a CenterNet-style head: one centre heatmap per class, trained with the penalty-reduced focal loss of CornerNet and CenterNet [59,60], and a width-height regression read at the centre. Decoding takes the local maxima of the heatmap (a 3 × 3 max-pool replaces NMS) and reads the box size there.

multitask.pyCenterNet focal loss and peak decoding ran

def centernet_focal(logits, gt, alpha=2, beta=4):
    """Penalty-reduced pixel-wise focal loss of CornerNet/CenterNet."""
    p = torch.sigmoid(logits).clamp(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4)
    pos = gt.eq(1).float()                          # exact peaks only
    neg_w = (1 - gt) ** beta
    loss = -(pos * (1 - p) ** alpha * torch.log(p) + (1 - pos) * neg_w * p ** alpha * torch.log(1 - p))
    return loss.sum() / pos.sum().clamp(min=1)


@torch.no_grad()
def decode_detections(ctr_logits, wh, k=10, thr=0.3):
    """Peaks = pixels equal to their 3x3 max-pool (a 'NMS-free' local-max filter)."""
    heat = torch.sigmoid(ctr_logits)
    peaks = heat * (F.max_pool2d(heat, 3, 1, 1) == heat)
    Cc, H, W = heat.shape
    scores, idx = peaks.flatten().topk(k)
    dets = []
    for s, i in zip(scores.tolist(), idx.tolist()):
        if s < thr:
            break
        c, rem = divmod(i, H * W); y, x = divmod(rem, W)
        bw, bh = wh[:, y, x].tolist()
        dets.append((c, s, np.array([x + .5 - bw / 2, y + .5 - bh / 2, x + .5 + bw / 2, y + .5 + bh / 2])))
    return dets
circle AP@0.5 = 0.960 AP@0.75 = 0.950 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.821 square AP@0.5 = 0.970 AP@0.75 = 0.947 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.821 triangle AP@0.5 = 0.979 AP@0.75 = 0.896 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.780 mean AP@0.5 = 0.970 AP@0.75 = 0.931 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.807

Almost every object is found (AP@0.5 = 0.97), and the drop to the COCO-style AP@[.5:.95] of 0.81 is localisation error at the strictest thresholds. This network has no sub-pixel offset head, unlike the full CenterNet [60], so the predicted centre is quantised to the pixel grid; on objects 10–25 pixels across, a one-pixel error in centre and size already costs about 0.1–0.25 IoU.

Exercises · §2
  1. Two 40 × 40 boxes are offset by 10 pixels horizontally and 10 vertically. What is their IoU? What offset along one axis alone gives IoU = 0.5?
    Show solution

    The intersection is 30 × 30 = 900 and the union 1,600 + 1,600 − 900 = 2,300, so IoU = 0.391. For a shift d along one axis the intersection is 40(40 − d) and the union 3,200 − 40(40 − d). Setting the ratio to 0.5 gives 40(40 − d) = 1,600/1.5 ≈ 1,066.7, so 40 − d = 26.7 and d ≈ 13.3 pixels. A box displaced by a third of its width already fails the 0.5 threshold, which is why AP at 0.75 and above is demanding.

  2. Explain why greedy NMS with threshold 0.5 can never output two correct boxes for two ground-truth objects whose boxes overlap with IoU 0.6, and give two remedies.
    Show solution

    Even perfect detections of the two objects have IoU 0.6 with each other. Whichever scores higher suppresses the other because 0.6 > 0.5. Remedies: Soft-NMS [66], which lowers the second score instead of removing the box so it can still be ranked and matched; or a detector trained with one-to-one assignment (DETR [63], YOLOv10 [71]) that does not produce duplicates and so needs no NMS. Raising the NMS threshold globally also works but lets duplicates through elsewhere.

  3. Using average_precision, compute AP@0.5 when the false positive at score 0.6 in the example is given score 0.99 instead. Explain the change.
    Show solution

    The ranking becomes FP, TP, TP, TP. Precision is 0, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4 at recall 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1; the monotone envelope is 0.75 everywhere, so AP = 0.75. A single confident false positive at the top of the ranking caps the precision achievable at every recall level. AP is a ranking metric: the same set of boxes with different scores gives a different AP.

    dets[2] = (1, .99, np.array([70, 70, 90, 90]))
print(round(average_precision(dets, gts, 0.5), 3))   # 0.75
  4. For γ = 2 and α = 0.25, compute the focal loss and cross-entropy for (a) a positive anchor with p = 0.1, (b) a negative anchor with p = 0.1. Which one dominates training, and how does that differ from plain CE?
    Show solution

    (a) Positive, pₜ = 0.1: CE = −ln 0.1 = 2.303; FL = 0.25 × 0.9² × 2.303 = 0.466. (b) Negative, pₜ = 0.9: CE = −ln 0.9 = 0.105; FL = 0.75 × 0.1² × 0.105 = 0.00079. Under CE the easy negative contributes 1/22 of the hard positive's loss, so 10⁵ easy negatives against a handful of positives dominate the total. Under FL the ratio is about 1/590, so the hard examples dominate. Note that α = 0.25 actually weights positives less; Lin et al. found that the best α decreases as γ increases, because the modulating factor already suppresses the easy negatives [58].

  5. A camera runs at 30 fps and the detector takes 22 ms per frame on the GPU. Resizing and normalisation take 4 ms on the CPU and NMS takes between 1 and 9 ms depending on the scene. Is the pipeline real-time? Suggest two changes.
    Show solution

    The budget is 33.3 ms. The worst case is 4 + 22 + 9 = 35 ms, which drops frames in crowded scenes even though the average case fits. Options: run preprocessing for frame t+1 on the CPU while the GPU processes frame t, which hides the 4 ms; cap the number of pre-NMS candidates by top-k before NMS, which bounds its cost; move to an NMS-free detector [71,72]; or reduce input resolution. Always measure the tail latency, not just the mean.

§3Image segmentation

Segmentation moves from one answer per object to one answer per pixel. Three formulations are in common use, and the clearest way to tell them apart is by what they say about a pixel [9]:

  • Semantic segmentation gives every pixel a class label. Two adjacent cars merge into one "car" region; there is no notion of individual objects.
  • Instance segmentation gives every detected object its own mask, class and score. Masks may overlap, and pixels that belong to no countable object (sky, road) are not labelled at all.
  • Panoptic segmentation gives every pixel both a class and an instance id, with no overlaps. Countable things (people, cars) get separate ids; amorphous stuff (sky, grass) gets one segment per class.

Columns 3 to 5 of Figure 2 show the three outputs for the same synthetic scenes: in the semantic map the two triangles of row 2 have the same colour; in the instance map they differ; the panoptic map carries both, and labels the background too.

3.1 Semantic segmentation

Fully convolutional networks. Long et al. observed that a classification network's fully connected layers can be rewritten as convolutions, so the network accepts any input size and outputs a coarse class map. Upsampling that map and fusing it with predictions from earlier, higher-resolution layers ("skip" connections) gave the first end-to-end trained dense predictor, the FCN [75]. Everything since addresses the same tension: classification needs large receptive fields and downsampling, while segmentation needs full-resolution boundaries.

  • Encoder–decoder with skips. U-Net mirrors the downsampling encoder with an upsampling decoder and concatenates encoder features at each resolution. It was designed for biomedical images with few training examples and remains the default architecture in medical imaging [76]. The network used throughout this article is a three-level U-Net.
  • Dilated (atrous) convolution. Spacing the taps of a 3 × 3 kernel r pixels apart enlarges the receptive field without downsampling or extra parameters [77]. DeepLab combined atrous convolution with atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP, parallel branches at several rates) and, in early versions, a fully connected CRF to sharpen boundaries [78]; DeepLabv3+ added a light decoder [79].
  • Global context. PSPNet pools the final feature map at several grid sizes and concatenates the upsampled results, so each pixel's prediction sees scene-level context: a boat is more likely on water than on a road [80].
  • Transformers. SegFormer pairs a hierarchical transformer encoder with a lightweight all-MLP decoder [81]; mask-classification models (§3.3) now unify semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation.

Losses. The default loss is pixel-wise cross-entropy. When the foreground is a tiny fraction of the image, as with lesions in medical scans, a model that predicts background everywhere achieves high pixel accuracy and low cross-entropy. The soft Dice loss, introduced with V-Net, directly optimises region overlap per class and so is insensitive to the size of the background [82]; it is often added to cross-entropy rather than used alone.

seg_losses.pywhy pixel accuracy and CE mislead on small objects ran

"""Pixel-wise cross-entropy vs. soft Dice on a small foreground object."""
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def soft_dice_loss(logits, target, eps=1.0):
    """1 - mean over classes of 2|P∩G| / (|P| + |G|), with soft P = softmax probabilities."""
    p = logits.softmax(1)                                    # (B, C, H, W)
    g = F.one_hot(target, p.shape[1]).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float()
    inter = (p * g).sum((0, 2, 3))
    denom = p.sum((0, 2, 3)) + g.sum((0, 2, 3))
    return 1 - ((2 * inter + eps) / (denom + eps)).mean()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    H = W = 64
    target = torch.zeros(1, H, W, dtype=torch.long); target[0, 30:34, 30:34] = 1     # 16 of 4096 pixels
    all_bg = torch.zeros(1, 2, H, W); all_bg[:, 0] = 8.0                            # predicts "background" everywhere
    perfect = torch.zeros(1, 2, H, W); perfect[:, 0] = 8.0; perfect[0, 0, 30:34, 30:34] = -8; perfect[0, 1, 30:34, 30:34] = 8
    for name, lg in [("all background", all_bg), ("perfect", perfect)]:
        acc = (lg.argmax(1) == target).float().mean().item()
        print(f"{name:<15} pixel acc {acc:.4f}  CE {F.cross_entropy(lg, target):.4f}  Dice loss {soft_dice_loss(lg, target):.4f}")
all background pixel acc 0.9961 CE 0.0316 Dice loss 0.4736 perfect pixel acc 1.0000 CE 0.0003 Dice loss 0.0200

Metric. The standard score is mean intersection over union: accumulate a confusion matrix over the whole test set, compute IoU = TP / (TP + FP + FN) for each class, and average over classes [6,7]. Accumulating over the dataset rather than averaging per-image IoUs matters, because small classes are absent from many images. Cityscapes, for example, has 5,000 finely annotated urban images and evaluates 19 classes [7]; the ADE20K scene-parsing benchmark uses 150 classes [8].

3.2 Instance segmentation

The dominant approach is "detect, then segment". Mask R-CNN adds a small fully convolutional branch to Faster R-CNN that predicts a 28 × 28 binary mask for each region of interest, one mask per class, with the class chosen by the box head [83]. Two details made it work. RoIAlign samples the feature map with bilinear interpolation at exact (non-rounded) positions, removing the quantisation of RoI pooling that misaligned masks by up to a feature-map cell. Decoupling mask and class prediction, using a per-pixel sigmoid per class instead of a softmax over classes, avoids competition between classes at the mask level [83]. One-stage alternatives avoid per-RoI processing: YOLACT predicts a set of prototype masks for the whole image and a coefficient vector per detection, and assembles each instance mask as a linear combination, reaching real-time speed [84]; SOLO assigns each instance to a grid cell by its centre and predicts a mask per cell [85]. Instance segmentation is scored with COCO AP exactly as detection is, but with mask IoU instead of box IoU [5].

recipepretrained Mask R-CNN inference with TorchVision recipe

import torch
from torchvision.io import read_image
from torchvision.models.detection import maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2, MaskRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_V2_Weights

weights = MaskRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_V2_Weights.DEFAULT           # COCO-trained, downloaded on first use
model = maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2(weights=weights).eval()
img = weights.transforms()(read_image("street.jpg"))
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([img])[0]                                    # boxes, labels, scores, masks
keep = out["scores"] > 0.5
masks = out["masks"][keep, 0] > 0.5                          # (N, H, W) boolean, one per instance
names = [weights.meta["categories"][i] for i in out["labels"][keep]]

3.3 Panoptic segmentation

Kirillov et al. defined panoptic segmentation in 2019 to unify the semantic ("stuff") and instance ("things") views: every pixel receives a (class, instance id) pair, segments may not overlap, and stuff classes have a single segment per image [9]. COCO's panoptic annotations use 80 thing and 53 stuff classes. They also defined the metric. Predicted and ground-truth segments of the same class are matched if their IoU exceeds 0.5, a threshold at which matches are provably unique because two non-overlapping segments cannot both overlap one ground-truth segment by more than half. Then

PQ = Σ_(p,g)∈TP IoU(p,g) / ( |TP| + ½|FP| + ½|FN| ) = SQ × RQ SQ = mean IoU of matched pairs (segmentation quality) RQ = |TP| / ( |TP| + ½|FP| + ½|FN| ) (recognition quality, an F1 score)

PQ is computed per class and averaged; reporting it separately for things and stuff (PQTh, PQSt) shows which half of the problem a method handles well.

seg_metrics.pymean IoU from a confusion matrix, and panoptic quality ran

"""Segmentation metrics from scratch: confusion-matrix mIoU and panoptic quality."""
import numpy as np


def confusion(pred, gt, n_cls, ignore=255):
    m = gt != ignore
    return np.bincount(n_cls * gt[m] + pred[m], minlength=n_cls ** 2).reshape(n_cls, n_cls)


def miou(conf):
    tp = np.diag(conf).astype(float)
    iou = tp / (conf.sum(0) + conf.sum(1) - tp + 1e-12)   # TP / (TP + FP + FN)
    return iou, iou[conf.sum(1) > 0].mean()               # ignore classes absent from GT


def panoptic_quality(pred_seg, gt_seg, pred_info, gt_info, n_cls):
    """pred_seg/gt_seg: (H,W) segment ids; *_info: {segment_id: class}.

    A predicted and a GT segment match iff same class and IoU > 0.5 (unique by
    construction, Kirillov et al. 2019).  Returns per-class PQ, SQ, RQ.
    """
    stats = {c: dict(tp=0, fp=0, fn=0, iou=0.0) for c in range(n_cls)}
    matched_p, matched_g = set(), set()
    for g, gc in gt_info.items():
        gm = gt_seg == g
        for p, pc in pred_info.items():
            if pc != gc:
                continue
            pm = pred_seg == p
            inter = np.logical_and(gm, pm).sum()
            if inter == 0:
                continue
            iou = inter / np.logical_or(gm, pm).sum()
            if iou > 0.5:
                stats[gc]["tp"] += 1; stats[gc]["iou"] += iou
                matched_p.add(p); matched_g.add(g)
    for g, gc in gt_info.items():
        if g not in matched_g:
            stats[gc]["fn"] += 1
    for p, pc in pred_info.items():
        if p not in matched_p:
            stats[pc]["fp"] += 1
    out = {}
    for c, s in stats.items():
        denom = s["tp"] + 0.5 * s["fp"] + 0.5 * s["fn"]
        if denom == 0:
            continue
        sq = s["iou"] / s["tp"] if s["tp"] else 0.0
        rq = s["tp"] / denom
        out[c] = dict(PQ=round(float(sq * rq), 3), SQ=round(float(sq), 3), RQ=round(rq, 3))
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    gt = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1], [2, 2, 2, 0], [2, 2, 2, 0]])
    pr = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1, 1], [2, 2, 0, 0], [2, 2, 2, 0]])
    iou, m = miou(confusion(pr.ravel(), gt.ravel(), 3))
    print("per-class IoU", iou.round(3), "mIoU", round(m, 3))
    # panoptic toy: two GT 'thing' segments of class 1, one predicted well, one missed,
    # plus one spurious prediction
    G = np.zeros((10, 10), int); G[1:5, 1:5] = 1; G[6:9, 6:9] = 2
    P = np.zeros((10, 10), int); P[1:5, 1:4] = 7; P[0:2, 7:9] = 8
    print(panoptic_quality(P, G, {7: 1, 8: 1}, {1: 1, 2: 1}, 2))
per-class IoU [0.714 0.8 0.833] mIoU 0.783 {1: {'PQ': 0.375, 'SQ': 0.75, 'RQ': 0.5}}

In the panoptic toy example the first object is found with IoU 0.75, the second is missed (one FN), and a spurious segment adds one FP: SQ = 0.75, RQ = 1/(1 + 0.5 + 0.5) = 0.5, so PQ = 0.375.

Architectures. Panoptic FPN attaches a semantic-segmentation branch to Mask R-CNN and merges the outputs with heuristics: paint instance masks in order of confidence, resolve overlaps in favour of the higher score, then fill the remaining pixels from the stuff prediction [86]. MaskFormer reframed all segmentation as mask classification: predict a set of N binary masks, each with a class label, using DETR-style set prediction [87]. Mask2Former restricted cross-attention to the predicted mask region and became the first single architecture to reach state-of-the-art results on semantic, instance and panoptic benchmarks [88]. Promptable foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) produce class-agnostic masks from points or boxes [89]; the generative and vision-language article in this series covers them.

3.4 Results on the toy world

The same network has a four-way semantic head (background plus three shapes). Instance and panoptic outputs are then derived with the Panoptic FPN-style heuristic: each detected box claims the pixels inside it whose semantic label agrees with its class, in order of decreasing score, and the rest becomes one background segment.

evaluate.pyheuristic panoptic merge from detections + semantics ran

def derive_panoptic(dets, sem_pred):
    """Heuristic merge (as in Panoptic FPN): paint instances by descending score.

    An instance's mask = pixels inside its box whose semantic label agrees with its class,
    minus pixels already claimed. Remaining pixels form one 'background' stuff segment.
    """
    H, W = sem_pred.shape
    seg = np.zeros((H, W), np.int64); info = {}
    for i, (c, s, b) in enumerate(sorted(dets, key=lambda d: -d[1])):
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = np.clip(np.round(b), 0, [W, H, W, H]).astype(int)
        m = np.zeros((H, W), bool); m[y1:y2, x1:x2] = True
        m &= (sem_pred == c + 1) & (seg == 0)
        if m.sum() >= 8:
            seg[m] = i + 1; info[i + 1] = c + 1          # panoptic class ids: 1..3 things
    bg = seg == 0
    seg[bg] = 1000; info[1000] = 0                       # 0 = background (stuff)
    return seg, info
semantic segmentation (500 held-out scenes) IoU[background]=1.000 IoU[circle]=0.944 IoU[square]=0.949 IoU[triangle]=0.943 mIoU = 0.959 panoptic quality background PQ = 0.996 (SQ = 0.996, RQ = 1.000) circle PQ = 0.909 (SQ = 0.934, RQ = 0.973) square PQ = 0.891 (SQ = 0.932, RQ = 0.956) triangle PQ = 0.900 (SQ = 0.937, RQ = 0.960) PQ (things) = 0.900 PQ (stuff) = 0.996 PQ (all) = 0.924

The heuristic fails in a characteristic place: when two objects of the same class overlap, the semantic map cannot say which pixel belongs to which, and the box-based split guesses. Learned instance masks (Mask R-CNN) or mask classification (Mask2Former) exist to resolve exactly this case.

Exercises · §3
  1. A test set has two images. In image A a "pole" class occupies 100 pixels and the prediction gets 90 of them right with no false positives. In image B the pole is absent but the model predicts 100 pole pixels. Compute the pole IoU (a) by accumulating the confusion matrix over the dataset, (b) by averaging per-image IoU, skipping images where the class is absent from both prediction and truth. Which is standard and why?
    Show solution

    (a) TP = 90, FN = 10, FP = 100, so IoU = 90/200 = 0.45. (b) Image A: 90/100 = 0.9. Image B: TP = 0 and FP = 100, so IoU = 0. The mean is 0.45 here by coincidence; change B's false positives to 10 pixels and dataset IoU becomes 90/110 = 0.82 while the per-image mean stays 0.45, because a few stray pixels in an image without poles count as a full failure. Accumulating over the dataset (a) is the convention of VOC and Cityscapes [6,7] because it weights errors by pixel count and avoids undefined or unstable per-image ratios for small classes.

  2. A 3 × 3 convolution with dilation rate r is stacked three times with rates 1, 2 and 4. What is the receptive field of one output pixel? Compare with three ordinary 3 × 3 convolutions.
    Show solution

    Each layer with rate r adds 2r to the receptive field: 1 + 2(1 + 2 + 4) = 15 pixels, versus 1 + 2 × 3 = 7 for three undilated layers, with the same parameter count and no downsampling. This exponential growth with rates 1, 2, 4, … is the design of Yu and Koltun's context module [77]. Rates must be chosen with care: using the same large rate repeatedly leaves "holes" (gridding), because the sampled positions never cover the pixels in between.

  3. Why does Mask R-CNN predict K masks per RoI and select the one for the predicted class, rather than a single mask with a K-way softmax per pixel?
    Show solution

    A per-pixel softmax makes classes compete inside the mask, so the mask branch would have to solve classification again at every pixel, and gradients from the wrong class would shape the mask. With K independent sigmoid masks, the box branch decides the class and the mask branch only has to answer "is this pixel part of the object", given the class. He et al. report a large gain in mask AP from this decoupling [83].

  4. Prove that with an IoU threshold above 0.5 each ground-truth segment can match at most one predicted segment, given that predicted segments do not overlap.
    Show solution

    Suppose predicted segments p₁ and p₂ (disjoint) both have IoU > 0.5 with ground truth g. IoU(p, g) > 0.5 implies |p ∩ g| > 0.5 |p ∪ g| ≥ 0.5 |g|. So each pᵢ covers more than half of g, and since they are disjoint, together they cover more than all of g: a contradiction. The same argument with roles swapped shows each prediction matches at most one ground truth, which is why panoptic quality needs no matching algorithm [9].

  5. A panoptic model detects 9 of 10 cars with average IoU 0.8, adds 3 false car segments, and labels the road with IoU 0.95. Compute PQ for "car" and "road" and the mean PQ. What would improve PQ most?
    Show solution

    Car: TP = 9, FN = 1, FP = 3, SQ = 0.8, RQ = 9/(9 + 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 1) = 9/11 = 0.818, PQ = 0.655. Road: its single segment is matched, so RQ = 1, SQ = 0.95 and PQ = 0.95. Mean PQ = 0.80. Removing the three false positives would raise car RQ to 9/9.5 = 0.947 and car PQ to 0.758; improving mask quality from 0.8 to 0.85 IoU would raise car PQ only to 0.695. For this model, recognition errors cost more than boundary errors.

§4Keypoints and pose estimation

Keypoint estimation localises a fixed, ordered set of landmarks on an object: the 17 body joints of the COCO keypoint format (nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles) [10], the 16 joints of MPII [11], 68 facial landmarks in the 300-W benchmark [90], or 21 hand landmarks [91,92]. Unlike detection, the output has a fixed structure per object, so it can be graded joint by joint. Human pose estimation is the most studied case: 2-D pose in the image plane, 3-D pose in metric space, and tracking of articulated motion over time.

4.1 Regression versus heatmaps

DeepPose regressed joint coordinates directly from a CNN, refining them with a cascade of crops [93]. Direct regression has to map a translation-equivariant feature map to absolute coordinates through fully connected layers, which wastes the convolution's structure. Tompson et al. instead predicted one heatmap per joint, trained to match a Gaussian centred on the true location [94], and this became the dominant representation. Convolutional pose machines refined heatmaps over several stages with intermediate supervision [95], stacked hourglass networks repeated bottom-up and top-down processing [96], SimpleBaselines showed that a ResNet followed by three deconvolution layers is a strong baseline [97], HRNet kept a high-resolution branch through the whole network, exchanging information with lower-resolution branches [98], and ViTPose showed that a plain vision transformer with a simple decoder scales well [99].

Heatmaps raise a decoding question. The argmax is quantised to the heatmap grid, often a quarter of input resolution, so a common trick shifts the argmax a quarter pixel toward the higher neighbour; DARK fits a Taylor expansion of the log-heatmap around the peak and refines the estimate further [100]. Integral regression replaces the argmax with a soft-argmax (the expected coordinate under a softmax of the heatmap), which is differentiable and so can be trained end to end with a coordinate loss [101].

kpt_utils.pyheatmaps, decoding, OKS, PCK and Procrustes-aligned MPJPE ran

"""Keypoint utilities: Gaussian heatmaps, decoding, OKS, PCK, Procrustes-aligned MPJPE."""
import numpy as np


def gaussian_heatmap(h, w, x, y, sigma=2.0):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:h, 0:w]
    return np.exp(-((xx - x) ** 2 + (yy - y) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2))


def decode_argmax(hm):
    """Integer argmax plus the classic quarter-pixel shift toward the higher neighbour."""
    h, w = hm.shape
    y, x = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(hm), hm.shape)
    px, py = float(x), float(y)
    if 0 < x < w - 1:
        px += 0.25 * np.sign(hm[y, x + 1] - hm[y, x - 1])
    if 0 < y < h - 1:
        py += 0.25 * np.sign(hm[y + 1, x] - hm[y - 1, x])
    return float(px), float(py)


def soft_argmax(hm, beta=10.0):
    """Differentiable expectation of coordinates under softmax(beta * heatmap)."""
    h, w = hm.shape
    p = np.exp(beta * (hm - hm.max())); p /= p.sum()
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:h, 0:w]
    return float((p * xx).sum()), float((p * yy).sum())


def oks(pred, gt, vis, area, kappa):
    """COCO object keypoint similarity for one person. pred/gt: (K,2)."""
    d2 = ((pred - gt) ** 2).sum(1)
    e = d2 / (2 * area * kappa ** 2 + np.spacing(1))
    m = vis > 0
    return float(np.exp(-e[m]).mean()) if m.any() else 0.0


def pck(pred, gt, ref_len, alpha=0.5):
    """Fraction of keypoints within alpha * ref_len (e.g. head size for PCKh@0.5)."""
    return float((np.linalg.norm(pred - gt, axis=1) <= alpha * ref_len).mean())


def procrustes_align(X, Y):
    """Similarity transform (s, R, t) that best maps X onto Y, both (J,3)."""
    mx, my = X.mean(0), Y.mean(0)
    X0, Y0 = X - mx, Y - my
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X0.T @ Y0)
    D = np.eye(3); D[2, 2] = np.sign(np.linalg.det(U @ Vt))  # no reflections
    R = U @ D @ Vt
    s = np.trace(np.diag(S) @ D) / (X0 ** 2).sum()
    return s * X0 @ R + my


def mpjpe(pred, gt):
    return float(np.linalg.norm(pred - gt, axis=1).mean())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hm = gaussian_heatmap(64, 48, 20.3, 31.7, sigma=2)
    print("argmax+shift:", decode_argmax(hm), " soft-argmax:", tuple(round(v, 2) for v in soft_argmax(hm)))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    gt = rng.uniform(0, 100, (17, 2)); pred = gt + rng.normal(0, 3, gt.shape)
    kappa = np.full(17, 2 * 0.072)   # COCO uses kappa_i = 2 sigma_i; sigma = 0.072 for elbows
    print("OKS (area 100^2):", round(oks(pred, gt, np.ones(17), 100 ** 2, kappa), 3))
    print("PCK@0.5, ref=10px:", round(pck(pred, gt, 10), 3))
    # 3D: a skeleton rotated, scaled and shifted then jittered
    J = rng.normal(0, 200, (17, 3))
    th = np.deg2rad(30); R = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th), 0], [np.sin(th), np.cos(th), 0], [0, 0, 1]])
    P = 1.1 * J @ R.T + np.array([50, -20, 300]) + rng.normal(0, 10, J.shape)
    print("MPJPE raw (mm): %.1f   PA-MPJPE (mm): %.1f" % (mpjpe(P, J), mpjpe(procrustes_align(P, J), J)))
argmax+shift: (20.25, 31.75) soft-argmax: (20.45, 31.69) OKS (area 100^2): 0.955 PCK@0.5, ref=10px: 0.647 MPJPE raw (mm): 349.5 PA-MPJPE (mm): 13.5

The soft-argmax result is biased toward the centre of the map (20.45 instead of 20.3) because, with β = 10, the softmax still puts small weights on every far-away pixel. Integral regression avoids the bias by normalising the heatmap itself rather than exponentiating a Gaussian-shaped target [101].

4.2 Multi-person pose: top-down and bottom-up

Top-down methods run a person detector, crop each box and estimate a single pose per crop; SimpleBaselines, HRNet and ViTPose are top-down [97–99]. They are accurate because every person is processed at a standard scale, but their cost grows with the number of people and they fail when the detector fails. Bottom-up methods detect all joints in the image at once and then group them into people. OpenPose predicts, besides joint heatmaps, part affinity fields: 2-D vector fields along each limb whose line integral scores whether two candidate joints belong to the same person, followed by greedy bipartite matching [102]. Associative embedding instead predicts a scalar "tag" per joint, trained so that joints of the same person have similar tags [103]. Bottom-up cost is nearly independent of the number of people, which suits crowded scenes.

4.3 Faces, hands and objects

The same machinery applies to other landmark sets. Face alignment localises facial landmarks for normalisation before recognition (§5.1), expression analysis and animation; a classic fast method uses a cascade of regression trees that runs in about a millisecond per face [104], and the 300-W challenge standardised a 68-point annotation and its evaluation [90]. Hands are harder: they are small, highly articulated and self-occluding. Simon et al. bootstrapped hand keypoint labels by triangulating detections across a multi-camera dome [91], and MediaPipe Hands runs a palm detector followed by a 21-landmark model in real time on mobile devices [92]. For rigid or articulated objects such as cars or robot arms, keypoints serve as an intermediate representation from which 6-DoF pose can be solved with perspective-n-point; the 3-D vision article in this series covers that geometry.

4.4 Evaluation

COCO scores keypoints with object keypoint similarity, an IoU analogue for points:

OKS = Σ_i exp( −d_i² / (2 s² κ_i²) ) · δ(v_i > 0) / Σ_i δ(v_i > 0)

Here dᵢ is the distance between predicted and true keypoint i, s² is the object's segment area, vᵢ is the visibility flag and κᵢ is a per-keypoint constant derived from how much human annotators disagree on that keypoint: hips are hard to place, eyes are easy [10]. AP is then computed exactly as for detection, with OKS thresholds in place of IoU. MPII uses PCKh, the percentage of keypoints within a fraction (usually 0.5) of the head segment length [11]. For 3-D pose the standard metric is the mean per-joint position error in millimetres, after aligning the root joint, and often also after a rigid Procrustes alignment (PA-MPJPE), which removes global rotation and scale errors and isolates articulation errors [12,105]. The example above shows how large the difference is: a correctly articulated skeleton that is rotated by 30° and shifted has a raw MPJPE of 350 mm but a PA-MPJPE of 13.5 mm.

4.5 3-D human pose and shape

Recovering 3-D joints from one image is ill-posed (many 3-D poses project to the same 2-D pose) and needs learned priors. Human3.6M provided the reference training and evaluation data: 3.6 million 3-D poses of 11 actors captured with motion capture [12]. Martinez et al. showed that a simple fully connected network that lifts detected 2-D joints to 3-D does surprisingly well, suggesting that much of the error in 3-D pose comes from 2-D detection [105]. Lifting over time with temporal convolutions exploits motion continuity and also allows semi-supervised training on unlabelled video via back-projection [106]. Beyond joints, parametric body models such as SMPL describe the full body surface with a low-dimensional shape vector and per-joint rotations [107], and HMR regresses SMPL parameters directly from an image, using an adversarial prior to keep the bodies plausible [108].

4.6 Tracking articulated motion

Per-frame pose estimates jitter and occasionally swap identities between people. Video pose pipelines therefore link poses across frames, often by matching boxes or keypoints between consecutive frames using flow or OKS similarity, as in the tracking baseline of Xiao et al. [97]; PoseTrack provides a benchmark for joint estimation and tracking in video [109]. Temporal filtering then smooths each keypoint trajectory. A Kalman filter with a constant-velocity model is the classic choice [110]. For interactive applications, where lag matters as much as jitter, the One Euro filter adapts its low-pass cut-off to the signal's speed: heavy smoothing when the point is still, light smoothing when it moves fast [111].

one_euro.pyspeed-adaptive smoothing of a keypoint track ran

"""One Euro filter (Casiez et al. 2012) for jittery per-frame keypoints."""
import numpy as np


class OneEuro:
    def __init__(self, freq, min_cutoff=1.0, beta=0.05, d_cutoff=1.0):
        self.freq, self.min_cutoff, self.beta, self.d_cutoff = freq, min_cutoff, beta, d_cutoff
        self.x = self.dx = None

    def _alpha(self, cutoff):
        tau = 1.0 / (2 * np.pi * cutoff)
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + tau * self.freq)

    def __call__(self, x):
        if self.x is None:
            self.x, self.dx = x, np.zeros_like(x)
            return x
        dx = (x - self.x) * self.freq
        self.dx = self.dx + self._alpha(self.d_cutoff) * (dx - self.dx)
        cutoff = self.min_cutoff + self.beta * np.abs(self.dx)   # fast motion -> higher cutoff, less lag
        self.x = self.x + self._alpha(cutoff) * (x - self.x)
        return self.x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    fps = 30; t = np.arange(0, 6, 1 / fps)
    truth = 100 * (t > 2) * np.minimum(t - 2, 1)              # wrist at rest, then moves 100 px in 1 s
    meas = truth + rng.normal(0, 3, t.size)                  # detector jitter, sigma = 3 px
    f = OneEuro(fps, min_cutoff=0.5, beta=0.05)
    euro = np.array([f(m) for m in meas])
    ma = np.convolve(meas, np.ones(9) / 9, mode="full")[:t.size]   # causal 9-frame moving average
    still, moving = t < 2, (t > 2) & (t < 3)
    for name, y in [("raw", meas), ("moving avg (9)", ma), ("One Euro", euro)]:
        jit = np.std(np.diff(y[still]))
        lag = np.abs(y[moving] - truth[moving]).mean()
        print(f"{name:<15} jitter at rest {jit:5.2f} px/frame   mean error while moving {lag:5.2f} px")
raw jitter at rest 3.30 px/frame mean error while moving 2.83 px moving avg (9) jitter at rest 0.44 px/frame mean error while moving 11.97 px One Euro jitter at rest 0.75 px/frame mean error while moving 2.31 px

The fixed moving average removes jitter but lags 12 pixels behind a fast movement; the One Euro filter keeps most of the jitter reduction at rest and actually tracks the moving wrist more closely than the raw detections. The video understanding and tracking article in this series covers multi-object tracking in full.

4.7 Results on the toy world

Each synthetic object has three keypoints (corners of squares and triangles, three extreme points of circles), and the network predicts three class-agnostic keypoint heatmaps. Decoding is top-down in miniature: for each object box, take the argmax of each heatmap inside the box.

mean OKS (kappa = 0.1) = 0.821 PCK@0.1 (of box side) = 0.918 objects = 971

Here κ = 0.1 is used for all keypoints and the PCK threshold is 10% of the larger box side, which for these objects is 1–3 pixels. About 7% of keypoints are off by more than 3 pixels. Only 5% of all keypoints are hidden under another shape, yet hidden keypoints account for 38% of those large errors: the generator labels every keypoint as visible, whereas COCO marks occluded and unlabelled keypoints with a visibility flag so that the metric and the loss can treat them differently [10].

Exercises · §4
  1. A heatmap at 1/4 of the input resolution is decoded with integer argmax. What is the worst-case and the expected (uniform) localisation error in input pixels along one axis, before and after the quarter-pixel shift?
    Show solution

    On the heatmap grid, integer argmax has error uniform on [−0.5, 0.5] cells: worst case 0.5 cells = 2 input pixels, mean absolute error 0.25 cells = 1 input pixel. The quarter-shift moves the estimate to ±0.25 within the cell depending on which neighbour is higher, so the error becomes uniform on [−0.25, 0.25]: worst case 1 input pixel, mean 0.5 input pixels. For a small person 64 pixels tall, a 2-pixel error is a few per cent of body height, which is why sub-pixel decoding such as DARK measurably improves COCO AP [100].

  2. Two predictions have the same 10-pixel error on every keypoint, one on a person of area 100² pixels and one of area 300². Using κ = 0.079 × 2 (COCO's shoulder constant), compute the OKS of each. Why is the area in the formula?
    Show solution

    OKS = exp(−d²/(2 s² κ²)) with κ = 0.158. For s² = 10⁴: exponent = 100 / (2 × 10⁴ × 0.02496) = 0.200, OKS = 0.818. For s² = 9 × 10⁴: exponent = 0.0223, OKS = 0.978. The same pixel error is a larger fraction of a small person's body, and annotators' disagreement also scales with object size, so the area makes OKS scale-invariant in the same way IoU is [10].

  3. A stadium image contains 80 people. A top-down model needs a 15 ms detector pass and 4 ms per person crop; a bottom-up model needs 60 ms for the whole image and 0.1 ms per person for grouping. Which is faster here, and at what crowd size do they break even?
    Show solution

    Top-down: 15 + 80 × 4 = 335 ms. Bottom-up: 60 + 80 × 0.1 = 68 ms. Break-even at 15 + 4n = 60 + 0.1n, so n ≈ 11.5. Below about a dozen people top-down is faster (and usually more accurate, since each person is processed at a standard scale); in crowds bottom-up wins. Batching the crops on a GPU changes the constant but not the linear dependence on n.

  4. Explain why PA-MPJPE can be much lower than MPJPE, and give a case where reporting only PA-MPJPE would hide an error that matters.
    Show solution

    Procrustes alignment solves for the rotation, scale and translation that best fit the prediction to the truth before measuring error, so any global error in those quantities is forgiven; only articulation (relative joint positions) is scored, as the 350 mm versus 13.5 mm example shows. If the application needs the body's orientation or distance from the camera, such as fall detection (is the person horizontal?) or a robot that must avoid a person, a model that gets the articulation right but the global orientation wrong looks excellent under PA-MPJPE and fails in use. Report both.

  5. In one_euro.py, set beta = 0. What happens to the error while moving, and why? What does beta control?
    Show solution

    With β = 0 the cut-off stays at min_cutoff = 0.5 Hz regardless of speed, so the filter becomes a fixed first-order low-pass filter and lags badly during the movement: running the script with β = 0 gives a mean error of 21.5 px while moving, worse than the 9-frame moving average. β scales how much the cut-off rises with the estimated speed: larger β means less lag during fast motion at the cost of more jitter during moderate motion. Casiez et al. recommend tuning min_cutoff first with the point at rest to remove jitter, then raising β until lag is acceptable [111].

§5Recognition and retrieval

Classification needs every class to be known at training time. Many recognition problems break that assumption: a face-unlock system must recognise its owner from a single enrolment photo, a shop must find a product in a catalogue that changes daily, and a moderation team must find re-uploads of a known image. These are solved by embedding images into a vector space where distance means "same identity" or "same content", and then comparing vectors. The open-set tasks in this section differ in what "same" means:

Task"Same" meansQuery → answerTypical metric
Face verificationsame personpair → yes/noTAR at fixed FAR
Face identificationsame personprobe → identity in a galleryrank-1 accuracy
Person re-identificationsame person, other cameraperson crop → ranked galleryCMC rank-1, mAP
Instance recognitionsame physical object or placephoto → matching imagesmAP (ROxford, GLDv2)
Visual similarity searchvisually or semantically alikeimage or text → nearest imagesRecall@K
Near-duplicate detectionsame source image, editedimage → copiesprecision at high recall

5.1 Learning an embedding

The contrastive loss pulls embeddings of matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart until they are at least a margin apart [112]. The triplet loss compares an anchor with a positive and a negative, requiring d(a, p) + m < d(a, n); FaceNet trained a 128-dimensional face embedding this way with online hard-negative mining and reported 99.63% accuracy on the LFW verification benchmark [113], up from the 97.35% of DeepFace a year earlier [114]. Mining matters: most random triplets already satisfy the margin and contribute no gradient. The batch-hard variant samples P identities × K images per batch and uses, for each anchor, the farthest positive and the closest negative in the batch [115].

A second family keeps a classification layer during training but normalises both features and class weights so that logits are cosines, then adds a margin that makes the target class harder to satisfy. SphereFace used a multiplicative angular margin [116], CosFace subtracts a margin from the cosine [117], and ArcFace adds an angular margin m to the angle between feature and target weight, with scale s (the paper uses s = 64, m = 0.5) [118]. At test time the classifier is discarded and the normalised feature is the embedding. A careful re-evaluation found that, under equal conditions, many newer metric-learning losses improve much less over the classic contrastive and triplet losses than originally reported [119], which is a reason to tune the data pipeline and mining before changing the loss.

ArcFace: L = −log exp(s·cos(θ_y + m)) / [ exp(s·cos(θ_y + m)) + Σ_(j≠y) exp(s·cos θ_j) ]

metric_learning.pyArcFace and batch-hard triplet, trained and tested on unseen identities ran

"""Embedding losses: ArcFace additive angular margin and batch-hard triplet loss.

A short experiment trains a tiny embedding net on synthetic 'identities' (each identity is
a fixed random texture seen under random crops, flips and brightness) and evaluates
verification on identities never seen in training.
"""
import math
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from retrieval_utils import tar_at_far, recall_at_k_and_map


class ArcFace(nn.Module):
    """logit_y = s * cos(theta_y + m); other logits = s * cos(theta_j)  (Deng et al. 2019)."""
    def __init__(self, dim, n_classes, s=64.0, m=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.W = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_classes, dim) * 0.01)
        self.s, self.m = s, m

    def forward(self, emb, labels):
        cos = F.linear(F.normalize(emb), F.normalize(self.W)).clamp(-1 + 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)
        theta = torch.acos(cos)
        target = torch.cos(theta + self.m)
        onehot = F.one_hot(labels, cos.shape[1]).bool()
        logits = torch.where(onehot, target, cos) * self.s
        return F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)


def batch_hard_triplet(emb, labels, margin=0.3):
    """For each anchor: hardest positive and hardest negative in the batch (Hermans et al. 2017)."""
    d = torch.cdist(emb, emb)
    same = labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]
    hardest_pos = (d * same).max(1).values
    hardest_neg = d.masked_fill(same, float("inf")).min(1).values
    return F.relu(hardest_pos - hardest_neg + margin).mean()


def identities(n_id, rng, size=36):
    from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
    return [torch.from_numpy(gaussian_filter(rng.random((3, size, size)), (0, 1.5, 1.5)).astype(np.float32) * 4 - 1.5)
            for _ in range(n_id)]


def view(tex, rng, out=32):
    y, x = rng.integers(0, tex.shape[1] - out + 1, 2)
    v = tex[:, y:y + out, x:x + out]
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        v = v.flip(2)
    return v * float(rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3)) + 0.05 * torch.from_numpy(rng.normal(size=tuple(v.shape)).astype(np.float32))


class EmbedNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        c = lambda i, o: nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(i, o, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(o), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))
        self.f = nn.Sequential(c(3, 32), c(32, 64), c(64, 128), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(128, dim))

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.normalize(self.f(x))


def train(loss_name, train_ids, rng, steps=500):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = EmbedNet(); head = ArcFace(64, len(train_ids), s=16.0, m=0.3)   # milder than the face-scale s=64, m=0.5
    params = list(net.parameters()) + (list(head.parameters()) if loss_name == "arcface" else [])
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(params, 2e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        ids = rng.choice(len(train_ids), 16, replace=False)
        lab = torch.tensor(np.repeat(ids, 4))                    # P=16 identities x K=4 views
        x = torch.stack([view(train_ids[i], rng) for i in lab.tolist()])
        e = net(x)
        loss = head(e, lab) if loss_name == "arcface" else batch_hard_triplet(e, lab)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return net


@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(net, test_ids, rng, views=6):
    net.eval()
    x = torch.stack([view(t, rng) for t in test_ids for _ in range(views)])
    lab = np.repeat(np.arange(len(test_ids)), views)
    e = net(x).numpy(); sim = e @ e.T
    iu = np.triu_indices(len(lab), 1)
    same = lab[iu[0]] == lab[iu[1]]
    tar, thr = tar_at_far(sim[iu][same], sim[iu][~same], far=1e-3)
    np.fill_diagonal(sim, -np.inf)                               # leave-one-out retrieval
    rec, mAP = recall_at_k_and_map(sim, lab, lab, ks=(1, 5))
    return tar, rec, mAP


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    train_ids, test_ids = identities(200, rng), identities(100, rng)
    # how much does the margin cost the target class? theta = 30 degrees
    th = math.radians(30)
    print(f"cos(30deg) = {math.cos(th):.3f}, with m=0.5 rad: cos(30deg + 28.6deg) = {math.cos(th + .5):.3f}")
    for name in ("untrained", "triplet", "arcface"):
        net = EmbedNet() if name == "untrained" else train(name, train_ids, rng)
        tar, rec, mAP = evaluate(net, test_ids, rng)
        print(f"{name:<10} unseen identities: TAR@FAR=1e-3 {tar:.3f}  R@1 {rec[1]:.3f}  R@5 {rec[5]:.3f}  mAP {mAP:.3f}")
cos(30deg) = 0.866, with m=0.5 rad: cos(30deg + 28.6deg) = 0.520 untrained unseen identities: TAR@FAR=1e-3 0.035 R@1 0.260 R@5 0.415 mAP 0.082 triplet unseen identities: TAR@FAR=1e-3 0.866 R@1 0.998 R@5 1.000 mAP 0.805 arcface unseen identities: TAR@FAR=1e-3 0.919 R@1 0.998 R@5 1.000 mAP 0.817

Both losses turn an embedding that barely separates unseen identities (the untrained network still gets some signal from raw colour statistics) into one where the nearest neighbour is almost always the same identity. The stricter TAR at FAR = 10⁻³ separates them more than Recall@K does; ArcFace is slightly ahead here, but on this toy problem and with one seed the difference is not meaningful. ArcFace used a milder scale and margin (s = 16, m = 0.3) than the face-recognition defaults, which did not converge in 500 steps from scratch in a first attempt.

5.2 Face verification

A face recognition pipeline detects the face, aligns it using a few landmarks (§4.3) to a canonical position, embeds it, and compares embeddings by cosine similarity. Verification ("is this the same person?") thresholds a single similarity; identification ("who is this?") searches a gallery. Because errors in the two directions have very different costs, results are reported as a true accept rate at a fixed false accept rate, for example TAR at FAR = 10⁻⁴, rather than as accuracy; LFW's original protocol of 6,000 balanced pairs is now saturated [13,118]. Face recognition also has well-documented demographic differentials: NIST's evaluation of 189 algorithms found false-positive rates that varied by factors of 10 to 100 across demographic groups for many algorithms [120], and earlier audits of commercial face analysis found large accuracy gaps by skin type and gender [121]. Thresholds therefore need to be set and audited per deployment population, a topic the evaluation article in this series covers.

retrieval_utils.pyperceptual hashes, TAR@FAR, Recall@K and mAP ran

def tar_at_far(genuine, impostor, far=1e-3):
    """True-accept rate at the threshold where the impostor accept rate equals `far`."""
    thr = np.quantile(impostor, 1 - far)
    return float((genuine > thr).mean()), float(thr)


def recall_at_k_and_map(sim, q_ids, g_ids, ks=(1, 5)):
    """sim: (Q,G) similarity; ids give identity labels. Returns Recall@K dict and mAP."""
    order = np.argsort(-sim, axis=1)
    hits = g_ids[order] == q_ids[:, None]
    rec = {k: float(hits[:, :k].any(1).mean()) for k in ks}
    aps = []
    for h in hits:
        if not h.any():
            continue
        ranks = np.nonzero(h)[0] + 1
        aps.append(np.mean(np.arange(1, len(ranks) + 1) / ranks))
    return rec, float(np.mean(aps))

5.3 Person re-identification

Re-identification matches a person across non-overlapping cameras, typically from a detector crop, so faces are small or invisible and clothing and body shape carry the identity. Market-1501, a standard benchmark, has 32,668 boxes of 1,501 identities from six cameras [14]. Results are reported as the cumulative matching characteristic (rank-k accuracy) and mAP over all correct matches in the gallery, because a person usually appears many times. A strong baseline combines an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet, identity classification and triplet loss, and a few training tricks such as random erasing and a batch-normalisation "neck" between the two losses [122]; re-ranking the gallery with k-reciprocal nearest neighbours improves mAP further at query time [123]. Ye et al. survey the field [124]. Re-ID is surveillance technology, and its deployment raises legal and ethical questions that are as important as its accuracy.

5.4 Instance recognition and visual similarity search

Instance recognition finds images of the same physical object or place, such as a specific building, painting or product, despite changes in viewpoint, lighting and occlusion. The classical pipeline detected local features such as SIFT [125], quantised them into a visual vocabulary for inverted-file search as in text retrieval [126,127], and verified candidates geometrically by fitting a homography or affine transform with RANSAC [128]. Deep descriptors replaced the hand-crafted parts: global descriptors from CNN feature maps with generalised-mean (GeM) pooling, fine-tuned without human labels from 3-D reconstructions [129], and learned local features with attention-based keypoint selection (DELF) for spatial verification [130]. The revisited Oxford and Paris benchmarks fixed annotation errors and added harder protocols [15], and Google Landmarks v2 scaled the problem to about 5 million images of 200,000 landmarks [131].

Visual similarity search relaxes "same object" to "looks alike" or "is about the same thing". General-purpose embeddings from self-supervised models such as DINOv2 [132], or from image-text models such as CLIP, which also allow text queries [133], work well without task-specific training; fine-tuning on in-domain pairs adapts them to a catalogue.

Searching millions of vectors

Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector, which costs O(N d) per query. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude in speed and memory [134,135]:

  • Inverted file (IVF). Cluster the database with k-means into nlist cells and, at query time, search only the nprobe nearest cells.
  • Product quantisation (PQ). Split each vector into M sub-vectors and replace each by the index of its nearest centroid in a small codebook, so a 128-dimensional float vector (512 bytes) becomes M bytes; distances are computed from look-up tables [136].
  • Graph indexes (HNSW). Build a hierarchical proximity graph and search it greedily from coarse to fine layers; very fast and accurate, at the cost of extra memory for the links [137].

ann_search.pyexact vs IVF vs IVF-PQ vs HNSW with FAISS ran

"""Exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour search with FAISS on 200k clustered vectors."""
import time
import numpy as np
import faiss

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n, nq, k = 128, 200_000, 1_000, 10
centres = rng.normal(0, 1, (100, d)).astype("float32")      # 100 loose 'semantic' clusters
sample = lambda m: (centres[rng.integers(0, 100, m)] + 0.8 * rng.normal(0, 1, (m, d))).astype("float32")
xb, xq = sample(n), sample(nq)                                 # queries are new draws, not copies
faiss.normalize_L2(xb); faiss.normalize_L2(xq)               # inner product = cosine similarity

flat = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d); flat.add(xb)
t = time.time(); _, gt = flat.search(xq, k); t_flat = time.time() - t

def report(name, index, bytes_per_vec):
    t = time.time(); _, I = index.search(xq, k); dt = time.time() - t
    recall = np.mean([len(set(I[i]) & set(gt[i])) / k for i in range(nq)])
    print(f"{name:<22} recall@10 {recall:.3f}  {dt / nq * 1e3:6.3f} ms/query  {bytes_per_vec:>4} B/vector")

print(f"{'Flat (exact)':<22} recall@10 1.000  {t_flat / nq * 1e3:6.3f} ms/query  {d * 4:>4} B/vector")
quant = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)
ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quant, d, 1024, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); ivf.train(xb); ivf.add(xb)
for nprobe in (1, 8, 32):
    ivf.nprobe = nprobe; report(f"IVF1024 nprobe={nprobe}", ivf, d * 4)
q2 = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)
ivfpq = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(q2, d, 1024, 16, 8, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); ivfpq.train(xb); ivfpq.add(xb)
ivfpq.nprobe = 32; report("IVF1024,PQ16 nprobe=32", ivfpq, 16)
hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); hnsw.add(xb)
hnsw.hnsw.efSearch = 64; report("HNSW32 efSearch=64", hnsw, d * 4 + 32 * 2 * 4)
Flat (exact) recall@10 1.000 0.782 ms/query 512 B/vector IVF1024 nprobe=1 recall@10 0.212 0.019 ms/query 512 B/vector IVF1024 nprobe=8 recall@10 0.914 0.097 ms/query 512 B/vector IVF1024 nprobe=32 recall@10 1.000 0.390 ms/query 512 B/vector IVF1024,PQ16 nprobe=32 recall@10 0.210 0.169 ms/query 16 B/vector HNSW32 efSearch=64 recall@10 0.946 0.244 ms/query 768 B/vector

Timings are single-threaded on the CPU this article was built on and indicate relative cost only. The pattern is the general one. IVF's recall is controlled by nprobe: probing 8 of 1,024 cells already finds 91% of the true neighbours at an eighth of the cost of exact search. PQ with 16 bytes per vector cuts memory 32-fold but, on its own, recovers only about a fifth of the exact top 10, because the compressed distances cannot separate neighbours that are nearly equidistant; production systems therefore re-rank a few hundred PQ candidates with exact distances. HNSW reaches high recall quickly but uses more memory than the raw vectors.

5.5 Duplicate and near-duplicate detection

Exact duplicates are found by hashing file bytes, but any re-encoding changes those bytes. Perceptual hashes summarise coarse image structure in a short bit string so that edited copies have nearby hashes in Hamming distance. The average hash thresholds an 8 × 8 thumbnail at its mean; the difference hash (dHash) compares horizontally adjacent pixels of a 9 × 8 thumbnail [138]; the DCT-based pHash keeps the signs of the low-frequency DCT coefficients relative to their median [139]. They are cheap, need no training and are robust to resizing, compression and small colour changes, but not to crops, rotations or flips, which change the thumbnail's layout. Learned copy-detection descriptors, trained with augmentations that mimic real edits, handle those transformations; the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge benchmarked them on a million-image reference set [140], and SSCD is a strong self-supervised descriptor for the task [141]. Duplicate detection is also a data-hygiene step: near-duplicates shared between training and test splits inflate reported accuracy.

retrieval_utils.pydHash and pHash ran

def dhash(img, n=8):
    """Difference hash: compare horizontally adjacent pixels of an (n, n+1) thumbnail."""
    g = resize(_gray(img), (n, n + 1), anti_aliasing=True)
    return (g[:, 1:] > g[:, :-1]).ravel()


def phash(img, n=8, hi=32):
    """DCT hash: low-frequency DCT block of a hi x hi thumbnail, thresholded at its median."""
    g = resize(_gray(img), (hi, hi), anti_aliasing=True)
    c = dct(dct(g, axis=0, norm="ortho"), axis=1, norm="ortho")[:n, :n]
    return (c > np.median(c)).ravel()


def hamming(a, b):
    return int(np.count_nonzero(a != b))
