Exercises · §5
  1. For an embedding with θ = 30° between a feature and its class weight, compute the ArcFace target logit with s = 64 and m = 0.5, and the logit without the margin. Why does the loss stay high even when the sample is already classified correctly?
    Show solution

    Without margin: 64 × cos 30° = 55.4. With margin: 64 × cos(30° + 28.6°) = 64 × 0.520 = 33.3 (the script prints cos values 0.866 and 0.520). If another class's weight is at, say, 50°, its logit is 64 × 0.643 = 41.1, which now exceeds the target logit, so the loss is large and the gradient keeps pulling the feature toward its class weight until θy + m is smaller than every other angle. Correct classification is not enough; the sample must be correct by an angular margin, which produces the compact clusters of Figure 11 [118].

  2. A face-unlock system is used 10 times a day by its owner. Suppose impostor attempts are rare, but a FAR of 10⁻³ per attempt is considered too high. Explain why TAR at FAR = 10⁻⁶ is the relevant figure, and what happens to TAR as the operating FAR is lowered.
    Show solution

    FAR is the probability that one impostor attempt succeeds. At 10⁻³, an attacker with a thousand different faces (for example in a photo collection) expects to unlock the device once; at 10⁻⁶ that needs a million. Lowering FAR means raising the similarity threshold (the 1 − FAR quantile of impostor scores), which also rejects more genuine attempts, so TAR falls; the curve of TAR against FAR (a ROC curve on a log FAR axis) shows the trade-off. Owners tolerate an occasional retry (TAR 0.98 means one failure in 50) much better than a security hole, so the threshold is set on the FAR side first.

  3. In Re-ID, a query has 4 correct matches in the gallery, ranked at positions 1, 3, 10 and 50. Compute rank-1, rank-5 and AP. Which metric reveals that the system misses most appearances?
    Show solution

    Rank-1 = 1 (the first result is correct), rank-5 = 1. AP = (1/1 + 2/3 + 3/10 + 4/50)/4 = (1 + 0.667 + 0.3 + 0.08)/4 = 0.512. CMC rank-k only asks whether some correct match appears in the top k; AP rewards finding all appearances early. For forensic search, where every sighting matters, mAP is the relevant metric, which is why Market-1501 reports both [14].

  4. A catalogue holds 50 million 512-dimensional float32 embeddings. How much RAM does a flat index need? Design an index that fits in 8 GB and say what it costs in recall and how you would recover it.
    Show solution

    Flat: 50 × 10⁶ × 512 × 4 bytes = 102.4 GB. IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes needs 50 × 10⁶ × 64 = 3.2 GB for codes plus 8 bytes per vector for ids (0.4 GB) and a small coarse quantiser, so about 3.6 GB. PQ distances are approximate, so recall@10 against the exact neighbours drops (the toy run shows how much with 16-byte codes). Recover it by retrieving several hundred candidates with PQ and re-ranking them with exact distances: the full vectors can stay on SSD or in a separate store, since only a few hundred are read per query [134,136].

  5. Using Figure 13, explain why the mirrored image has a Hamming distance of about 32 bits for dHash. How would you make a hash-based duplicate detector mirror-invariant?
    Show solution

    dHash compares each pixel with its right-hand neighbour. Mirroring reverses the row order, so a "brighter than the neighbour" bit becomes "darker than the neighbour" at the mirrored position, and the resulting bits are nearly uncorrelated with the original: about half (32 of 64) differ, as for an unrelated image. Two fixes: index both the hash of the image and the hash of its mirror (or take the minimum distance over both at query time), or use a learned descriptor trained with flips as augmentation [141]. The same reasoning applies to crops and rotations, for which hashing the image at several crops or angles quickly becomes more expensive than a learned descriptor.

§6Motion analysis (overview)

Every task so far looks at one image. Video adds time, and with it a new kind of output: how things move. This section surveys the motion tasks at overview depth and shows the one algorithm every practitioner should be able to write from scratch, optical flow; the video understanding and tracking article in this series treats temporal models, tracking and video benchmarks in full.

6.1 Optical flow

Optical flow assigns each pixel a 2-D displacement (u, v) to its position in the next frame. Assuming that a point keeps its brightness as it moves, I(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = I(x, y, t), and linearising for small motion gives the optical flow constraint

I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0

This is one equation in two unknowns per pixel: only the component of motion along the image gradient is observable, the aperture problem. Horn and Schunck resolved it globally by adding a smoothness penalty on the flow field [142]. Lucas and Kanade resolved it locally by assuming constant flow in a small window and solving the resulting least-squares system, which is well conditioned only where the window contains gradients in two directions (corners and texture) [143]. Both rely on small motion, so practical implementations work coarse to fine on an image pyramid; Farnebäck's method, available in OpenCV, approximates each neighbourhood by a quadratic polynomial and estimates displacement from how the polynomial shifts [144].

flow_lk.pydense Lucas–Kanade from scratch, checked against a known shift and OpenCV ran

"""Dense Lucas-Kanade optical flow from scratch, checked against a known shift and OpenCV."""
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter, gaussian_filter, shift as nd_shift


def lucas_kanade(I0, I1, win=9, tau=1e-2):
    """One-scale LK: solve [sum IxIx, sum IxIy; sum IxIy, sum IyIy] [u v]^T = -[sum IxIt, sum IyIt]."""
    Iy, Ix = np.gradient(I0)
    It = I1 - I0
    Sxx = uniform_filter(Ix * Ix, win); Syy = uniform_filter(Iy * Iy, win)
    Sxy = uniform_filter(Ix * Iy, win)
    Sxt = uniform_filter(Ix * It, win); Syt = uniform_filter(Iy * It, win)
    det = Sxx * Syy - Sxy ** 2
    # smallest eigenvalue of the structure tensor; near zero = aperture problem (edge or flat region)
    lam_min = (Sxx + Syy) / 2 - np.sqrt(((Sxx - Syy) / 2) ** 2 + Sxy ** 2)
    ok = lam_min > tau * lam_min.max()
    u = np.where(ok, (-Syy * Sxt + Sxy * Syt) / np.where(ok, det, 1), 0)
    v = np.where(ok, (Sxy * Sxt - Sxx * Syt) / np.where(ok, det, 1), 0)
    return u, v, ok


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    I0 = gaussian_filter(rng.random((128, 128)), 3)
    I0 = (I0 - I0.min()) / (I0.max() - I0.min())
    true_u, true_v = 0.6, -0.3                         # sub-pixel motion, small enough for one-scale LK
    I1 = nd_shift(I0, (true_v, true_u), order=3, mode="reflect")
    u, v, ok = lucas_kanade(I0, I1)
    c = (slice(16, -16),) * 2
    epe = np.sqrt((u[c] - true_u) ** 2 + (v[c] - true_v) ** 2)[ok[c]].mean()
    print(f"LK  median flow = ({np.median(u[c][ok[c]]):.3f}, {np.median(v[c][ok[c]]):.3f})  EPE = {epe:.3f} px on {ok[c].mean():.0%} of pixels")
    import cv2
    f = cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback((I0 * 255).astype(np.uint8), (I1 * 255).astype(np.uint8),
                                     None, 0.5, 3, 15, 3, 5, 1.2, 0)
    epe_cv = np.sqrt((f[..., 0][c] - true_u) ** 2 + (f[..., 1][c] - true_v) ** 2).mean()
    print(f"Farneback mean flow = ({f[...,0][c].mean():.3f}, {f[...,1][c].mean():.3f})  EPE = {epe_cv:.3f} px")
LK median flow = (0.612, -0.305) EPE = 0.035 px on 100% of pixels Farneback mean flow = (0.598, -0.304) EPE = 0.011 px
disc (true 3.0, 2.0): Farneback (3.00, 2.00) LK (1.08, 0.98) background (true -1.0, 0.0): Farneback (-0.99, 0.00) LK (0.00, 0.00)

Run on the background alone, the same one-scale code recovers the −1 pixel pan almost exactly; it fails in the composite only because the sharper disc texture sets a conditioning threshold that the smooth background cannot meet. That is the aperture problem in practice: what counts as "enough texture" is relative.

Learned flow took over once synthetic training data made supervision possible. FlowNet trained an encoder-decoder CNN end to end on rendered "flying chairs" [145]. RAFT builds a 4-D correlation volume between all pairs of pixels and refines a single high-resolution flow field with a recurrent update operator; on the Sintel final pass it reported an end-point error of 2.855 pixels, a 30% reduction over the best published result at the time [146]. Flow is evaluated by the average end-point error, the Euclidean distance between predicted and true vectors, on benchmarks with dense ground truth such as Middlebury [16] and the rendered MPI-Sintel [17].

6.2 Action and gesture recognition

Action recognition classifies a clip ("playing violin", "opening a door"). The main architecture families are:

  • Two-stream networks: one CNN on RGB frames for appearance, one on stacked optical flow for motion, fused late [147]. Temporal segment networks sample short snippets across the whole video and aggregate their predictions, which models long-range structure cheaply [148].
  • Frame CNN + recurrent network: per-frame features fed to an LSTM [149].
  • 3-D convolution over space and time: C3D [150]; I3D "inflated" pretrained 2-D ImageNet filters into 3-D and was introduced together with the Kinetics dataset [18,151], whose first release had 400 human action classes with at least 400 clips each [18]. SlowFast pairs a low-frame-rate pathway for appearance with a high-frame-rate, lightweight pathway for motion [152].
  • Video transformers: TimeSformer factorises attention into separate temporal and spatial steps ("divided" attention) [153]; VideoMAE pretrains by reconstructing heavily masked video tubes [154].

Datasets differ in how much motion matters. Many Kinetics classes can be guessed from one frame (a swimming pool implies swimming), whereas Something-Something was designed so that classes such as "pushing something from left to right" can only be told apart by their temporal order [155]. Gesture recognition is the same problem for hand and body gestures used as commands, for example the 27 classes of the Jester dataset [156]; it is often run on keypoints rather than pixels, using graph convolutions over the skeleton across time (ST-GCN) [157], which ties this section back to §4.

recipeclip-level inference with a Kinetics-400 R(2+1)D model; decoding and shapes checked with random weights recipe

import torch
from torchcodec.decoders import VideoDecoder                 # TorchVision 0.29 no longer has read_video
from torchvision.models.video import r2plus1d_18, R2Plus1D_18_Weights

weights = R2Plus1D_18_Weights.DEFAULT                        # trained on Kinetics-400
model = r2plus1d_18(weights=weights).eval()
dec = VideoDecoder("clip.mp4")
idx = torch.linspace(0, dec.metadata.num_frames - 1, 16).long().tolist()   # 16 frames, uniformly (TSN-style)
frames = dec.get_frames_at(indices=idx).data                 # (T, C, H, W) uint8
clip = weights.transforms()(frames).unsqueeze(0)             # (1, C, T, H, W)
with torch.no_grad():
    probs = model(clip).softmax(-1)[0]
top = probs.topk(5)
print([(weights.meta["categories"][i], round(p.item(), 3)) for p, i in zip(top.values, top.indices)])

6.3 Motion segmentation, temporal modelling and event detection

Motion segmentation separates independently moving regions. With a static camera the classic tool is background subtraction: model each pixel's colour over time, for example as an adaptive mixture of Gaussians, and flag pixels that do not fit [158,159] (OpenCV's createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2 implements the latter). With a moving camera, pixels are instead grouped by the consistency of their motion, for example by clustering long point trajectories [160].

Temporal modelling beyond the clip handles videos minutes or hours long. Temporal convolutional networks label every frame (action segmentation) with dilated 1-D convolutions over time [161]. Temporal action detection is to video what object detection is to images: find the start, end and class of each action instance in an untrimmed video, scored with temporal IoU and mAP on benchmarks such as THUMOS and ActivityNet [162,163]. Proposal methods such as BMN score every candidate (start, end) pair densely [164], the temporal analogue of anchors. Video event and anomaly detection flags rare events, such as accidents or fights in surveillance footage, often with only video-level labels; Sultani et al. framed it as multiple-instance learning over video segments [165].

Exercises · §6
  1. At a pixel on a long vertical edge, Ix = 0.2, Iy = 0 and It = −0.1. What can you say about (u, v)? What does the Lucas–Kanade structure tensor look like in a window along this edge, and how does lucas_kanade handle it?
    Show solution

    The constraint gives 0.2u − 0.1 = 0, so u = 0.5 and v is undetermined: motion along the edge is invisible. Over a window along the edge, ΣIx² > 0 but ΣIy² ≈ ΣIxIy ≈ 0, so the 2 × 2 matrix has one near-zero eigenvalue and is singular. lucas_kanade computes the smallest eigenvalue and marks such pixels as unreliable (ok = False), returning zero flow there; Horn–Schunck would instead fill in v from smoother neighbours [142].

  2. The one-scale LK estimate for the disc in Figure 14 is about (1.1, 1.0) instead of (3, 2). How many pyramid levels with a factor of 2 are needed so that the motion at the coarsest level is below 1 pixel? Why does that help?
    Show solution

    The motion magnitude is √(3² + 2²) ≈ 3.6 px. Halving per level gives 1.8 px at level 1 and 0.9 px at level 2, so three levels (original plus two coarser) are needed. At the coarsest level the linearisation of brightness constancy is valid, so LK estimates the motion well; that estimate is doubled, used to warp the next finer level, and only the small residual motion is estimated there. This coarse-to-fine scheme is what OpenCV's pyramidal LK and Farnebäck implement.

  3. A model reaches 80% top-1 accuracy on a Kinetics-style dataset using only a single frame per video. What does that suggest about the dataset, and how would you test whether a video model actually uses motion?
    Show solution

    It suggests that many classes are recognisable from scene and object context alone. Tests: evaluate on shuffled or reversed frames (a model that uses temporal order should degrade, especially for classes like "opening" versus "closing"); evaluate on a dataset built to require temporal reasoning, such as Something-Something [155]; or compare against a single-frame baseline per class to find where the temporal model actually helps.

  4. Temporal action detection is "object detection in 1-D". Map each of these image-detection concepts to its temporal counterpart: anchor box, IoU, NMS, COCO AP.
    Show solution

    Anchor box → a reference temporal segment (start, duration) at each time step, or a dense (start, end) grid as in BMN [164]. IoU → temporal IoU, the length of the intersection of two intervals divided by the length of their union. NMS → temporal NMS over overlapping segments. COCO AP → mAP averaged over temporal IoU thresholds, as in ActivityNet (0.5 to 0.95) [163].

§7One backbone, many heads

The sections above present the tasks separately, but the methods share most of their machinery. A modern vision system is usually a pretrained backbone, a neck that produces multi-scale features (an FPN or a U-Net decoder), and small task-specific heads. Mask R-CNN is literally a detector with a mask head, and its keypoint variant adds a keypoint head to the same network [83]; Panoptic FPN adds a semantic head [86]; CenterNet predicts boxes, 3-D properties and human pose from the same centre-point representation [60]. The table makes the correspondences explicit.

IdeaClassificationDetectionSegmentationPoseRetrieval
Output unitimageboxpixel / maskkeypointvector
Overlap measure—box IoUmask IoUOKScosine similarity
Ranking metricmAP (multi-label)AP over IoU thresholdsmask AP, PQAP over OKS thresholdsmAP, Recall@K
Imbalance fixASL, re-weightingfocal lossDice, class weightspenalty-reduced focalhard-negative mining
Duplicate handling—NMS / set matchingmask merginggroupingre-ranking

The toy network used throughout this article is a minimal instance of the pattern: one encoder-decoder and five 1 × 1 heads, trained jointly by summing the losses. Here is all of it.

multitask.pyone U-Net, five heads, trained on synthetic scenes on a CPU ran

"""One small backbone, five task heads, trained on synthetic shapes (CPU, a few minutes).

Heads: multi-label classification, CenterNet-style anchor-free detection
(centre heatmap + box size), semantic segmentation, and per-class keypoint heatmaps.
Instance and panoptic outputs are then *derived* from detections + semantics.
"""
import time
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from shapes import make_scene, multihot, N_KPT

torch.manual_seed(0)
S, C = 64, 3            # image size, number of thing classes


def targets(scene, sigma=1.5):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:S, 0:S]
    ctr = np.zeros((C, S, S), np.float32)
    wh = np.zeros((2, S, S), np.float32); wh_mask = np.zeros((S, S), np.float32)
    kpt = np.zeros((N_KPT, S, S), np.float32)
    for o in scene["objects"]:
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = o["box"]
        ix, iy = int((x1 + x2) / 2), int((y1 + y2) / 2)   # integer peak so the target hits 1.0
        g = np.exp(-((xx - ix) ** 2 + (yy - iy) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2))
        ctr[o["cls"]] = np.maximum(ctr[o["cls"]], g)
        wh[:, iy, ix] = (x2 - x1, y2 - y1); wh_mask[iy, ix] = 1
        for k, (kx, ky) in enumerate(np.clip(np.round(o["kpts"]), 0, S - 1)):
            kpt[k] = np.maximum(kpt[k], np.exp(-((xx - kx) ** 2 + (yy - ky) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2)))
    return ctr, wh, wh_mask, kpt


def make_batch(rng, n):
    xs, ys = [], {k: [] for k in ("ml", "sem", "ctr", "wh", "whm", "kpt")}
    scenes = []
    for _ in range(n):
        s = make_scene(rng); scenes.append(s)
        ctr, wh, whm, kpt = targets(s)
        xs.append(s["image"].transpose(2, 0, 1))
        for k, v in zip(ys, (multihot(s), s["semantic"], ctr, wh, whm, kpt)):
            ys[k].append(v)
    t = {k: torch.from_numpy(np.stack(v)) for k, v in ys.items()}
    return torch.from_numpy(np.stack(xs)).float(), t, scenes


def block(i, o):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(i, o, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(o), nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
                         nn.Conv2d(o, o, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(o), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))


class TinyUNet(nn.Module):
    """Encoder-decoder with skip connections; every dense head reads the full-res decoder map."""
    def __init__(self, w=24):
        super().__init__()
        self.e1, self.e2, self.e3 = block(3, w), block(w, 2 * w), block(2 * w, 4 * w)
        self.d2, self.d1 = block(6 * w, 2 * w), block(3 * w, w)
        self.cls = nn.Linear(4 * w, C)                  # image-level head on pooled bottleneck
        self.sem = nn.Conv2d(w, C + 1, 1)               # +1 for background
        self.ctr = nn.Conv2d(w, C, 1)                   # one centre heatmap per class
        self.wh = nn.Conv2d(w, 2, 1)                    # box width/height at centres
        self.kpt = nn.Conv2d(w, N_KPT, 1)               # keypoint heatmaps
        nn.init.constant_(self.ctr.bias, -2.19)         # prior p=0.1, as in RetinaNet/CenterNet
        nn.init.constant_(self.kpt.bias, -2.19)

    def forward(self, x):
        f1 = self.e1(x)
        f2 = self.e2(F.max_pool2d(f1, 2))
        f3 = self.e3(F.max_pool2d(f2, 2))
        d2 = self.d2(torch.cat([F.interpolate(f3, scale_factor=2), f2], 1))
        d1 = self.d1(torch.cat([F.interpolate(d2, scale_factor=2), f1], 1))
        return dict(ml=self.cls(f3.mean((2, 3))), sem=self.sem(d1), ctr=self.ctr(d1),
                    wh=self.wh(d1), kpt=self.kpt(d1))


def centernet_focal(logits, gt, alpha=2, beta=4):
    """Penalty-reduced pixel-wise focal loss of CornerNet/CenterNet."""
    p = torch.sigmoid(logits).clamp(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4)
    pos = gt.eq(1).float()                          # exact peaks only
    neg_w = (1 - gt) ** beta
    loss = -(pos * (1 - p) ** alpha * torch.log(p) + (1 - pos) * neg_w * p ** alpha * torch.log(1 - p))
    return loss.sum() / pos.sum().clamp(min=1)


def total_loss(out, t):
    l_ml = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(out["ml"], t["ml"])
    l_sem = F.cross_entropy(out["sem"], t["sem"])
    l_ctr = centernet_focal(out["ctr"], t["ctr"])
    m = t["whm"].unsqueeze(1)
    l_wh = (F.l1_loss(out["wh"], t["wh"], reduction="none") * m).sum() / m.sum().clamp(min=1)
    l_kpt = centernet_focal(out["kpt"], t["kpt"])
    return l_ml + l_sem + l_ctr + 0.1 * l_wh + l_kpt, dict(ml=l_ml, sem=l_sem, ctr=l_ctr, wh=l_wh, kpt=l_kpt)


@torch.no_grad()
def decode_detections(ctr_logits, wh, k=10, thr=0.3):
    """Peaks = pixels equal to their 3x3 max-pool (a 'NMS-free' local-max filter)."""
    heat = torch.sigmoid(ctr_logits)
    peaks = heat * (F.max_pool2d(heat, 3, 1, 1) == heat)
    Cc, H, W = heat.shape
    scores, idx = peaks.flatten().topk(k)
    dets = []
    for s, i in zip(scores.tolist(), idx.tolist()):
        if s < thr:
            break
        c, rem = divmod(i, H * W); y, x = divmod(rem, W)
        bw, bh = wh[:, y, x].tolist()
        dets.append((c, s, np.array([x + .5 - bw / 2, y + .5 - bh / 2, x + .5 + bw / 2, y + .5 + bh / 2])))
    return dets


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    model = TinyUNet()
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    steps, bs = 1200, 32
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=3e-3, total_steps=steps)
    t0 = time.time()
    for step in range(steps):
        x, t, _ = make_batch(rng, bs)
        loss, parts = total_loss(model(x), t)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); sched.step()
        if step % 250 == 0 or step == steps - 1:
            print(f"step {step:4d} loss {loss.item():.3f} " +
                  " ".join(f"{k}={v.item():.3f}" for k, v in parts.items()), flush=True)
    print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), "multitask.pt")
step 0 loss 20.900 ml=0.682 sem=1.618 ctr=9.326 wh=37.628 kpt=5.511 step 250 loss 2.018 ml=0.343 sem=0.282 ctr=0.516 wh=3.899 kpt=0.487 step 500 loss 1.166 ml=0.098 sem=0.069 ctr=0.295 wh=4.035 kpt=0.300 step 750 loss 0.616 ml=0.058 sem=0.021 ctr=0.120 wh=2.276 kpt=0.189 step 1000 loss 0.490 ml=0.042 sem=0.020 ctr=0.125 wh=1.187 kpt=0.185 step 1199 loss 0.390 ml=0.022 sem=0.017 ctr=0.095 wh=1.270 kpt=0.128 trained in 1525s

Training ran for 1,200 steps of 32 freshly generated scenes on a 4-core CPU. Because every batch is new, there is no overfitting in the usual sense, and the held-out numbers reported in §1–§4 come from 500 scenes generated with a different seed:

[multilabel] AP[circle ] = 1.000 AP[square ] = 1.000 AP[triangle] = 1.000 mAP = 1.000 exact-match accuracy at 0.5 = 0.966 [detection] circle AP@0.5 = 0.960 AP@0.75 = 0.950 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.821 square AP@0.5 = 0.970 AP@0.75 = 0.947 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.821 triangle AP@0.5 = 0.979 AP@0.75 = 0.896 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.780 mean AP@0.5 = 0.970 AP@0.75 = 0.931 AP@[.5:.95] = 0.807 [semantic] IoU[background]=1.000 IoU[circle]=0.944 IoU[square]=0.949 IoU[triangle]=0.943 mIoU = 0.959 [panoptic] background PQ = 0.996 (SQ = 0.996, RQ = 1.000) circle PQ = 0.909 (SQ = 0.934, RQ = 0.973) square PQ = 0.891 (SQ = 0.932, RQ = 0.956) triangle PQ = 0.900 (SQ = 0.937, RQ = 0.960) PQ (things) = 0.900 PQ (stuff) = 0.996 PQ (all) = 0.924 [keypoints] mean OKS (kappa = 0.1) = 0.821 PCK@0.1 (of box side) = 0.918 objects = 971

Two lessons carry over to real systems. First, the heads compete for the backbone's capacity and the loss weights matter: here the box-size L1 loss is in pixels and would dominate the sum without its 0.1 weight. Second, the derived outputs are only as good as their inputs: panoptic quality for things is lower than semantic IoU because every detection error becomes a segment error, which is the argument for training masks directly.

§8Capstone project

Extend the toy world into a small but complete benchmark, using only the code in this article.

  1. Harder data. Add a fourth class (for example, a hollow ring that looks like a circle at low resolution, a fine-grained confusion), scale variation from 4 to 30 pixels, and scenes with up to eight objects. Report how per-class AP@0.5 and AP@[.5:.95] change.
  2. A proper instance head. Replace the box-plus-semantics heuristic with a learned instance representation: either a per-pixel offset to the object centre (pixels are grouped by the centre they vote for) or a small mask head on RoIAligned features (torchvision.ops.roi_align). Compare PQTh with the heuristic on scenes where same-class objects touch.
  3. Visibility-aware keypoints. Make the generator emit a visibility flag for keypoints hidden under other shapes, exclude them from the OKS denominator, and predict visibility with an extra head.
  4. Retrieval. Treat each scene's set of shapes and colours as its "identity", embed scenes with the pooled bottleneck features, and measure Recall@1 for finding the same scene after flips, crops and noise. Index 100,000 scenes with FAISS and compare IVF, IVF-PQ with re-ranking, and HNSW at equal recall.
  5. Motion. Animate the shapes with constant velocities, estimate flow with Farnebäck and with your own pyramidal Lucas–Kanade, and evaluate EPE against the generator's known velocities, separately on object interiors, boundaries and occluded regions.
Show solution outline

(1) Fine-grained confusion appears as cross-class false positives: the ring and circle APs both fall and their confusion is visible in the semantic confusion matrix. Small objects reduce AP@[.5:.95] far more than AP@0.5, because a one-pixel error on a 4-pixel object is a large IoU loss; a sub-pixel offset head, as in CenterNet [60], recovers much of it. (2) Centre-offset voting separates touching same-class objects that the heuristic merges, so RQ for things should rise most; the RoIAlign mask head behaves like Mask R-CNN [83] and is more robust when centres are close. (3) Excluding invisible points removes the 38% of large errors that came from hidden keypoints and makes OKS reflect what the network can see, as in COCO [10]. (4) Pooled features of a network trained on scene labels are not invariant to flips unless trained to be; adding a triplet loss on augmented pairs (§5.1) is the fix, and PQ codes with exact re-ranking of the top 100 typically approach exact recall at a small fraction of the memory [136]. (5) Errors concentrate at occlusion boundaries, where brightness constancy fails because pixels appear or disappear; one-scale LK fails for speeds above about one pixel per frame, and a three-level pyramid fixes most of that.

Part of a series on computer vision. Companion articles cover generative and vision-language models, 3-D vision, production engineering, evaluation and reliability, application domains, and video understanding and tracking. All code blocks marked “ran” were executed with the library versions listed in the introduction; outputs are reproduced verbatim.
